blocks.x: This is an interview, first reel, and we're doing it today, what's today, February what?
1961, it's a Friday, and we're at 1816 on Saga Street. And that's your home, let's hear your name. What's your name?
Alba Giles is my name.
That's your whole name?
Alba Giles.
And let's get your name.
Evelyn Giles. Evelyn F. Giles.
And your Mrs. Giles, wife.
And Marjorie Zander. And Dick Allen.

So, let's see. I think we've got your birth date and all that stuff about when you got started. I wanted to get you a little more about your grandfather. What was his name? My grandfather. Frank Giles.
Frank Giles. I see. And who did he play with?
Frank Giles.
I don't know who he played with, but he played, definitely they told me, in the old Civil War, he played the drums. But it was so far back concerning that the bands he played with, I never knew.
You didn't know which side, whether it was the United States or the Confederacy or?
Well he played with the South. He played with the North. He played with the North. I see. What about your father? He played with the band.
Don Witt. Joe Gabrella, Kester. And he was hired, he lived in Thibodeau, but he was hired in different bands.

From New Orleans. On days like Carnival and the other. He was hired. He was hired in different bands from New Orleans. On days like Carnival and the other. He was hired in different bands from New Orleans. On days like Carnival and other days that they had big events and called for a lot of bands.
Did Joe Gabriel have a brass band, Gabriel?
Yeah, he had orchestra and a brass band. Now that's a guy you should interview too. He's in Thibodeau.
He's so sick, I don't know if we can do it or not.
We went out to see him one time. Oh, I see.

He has fainting spells now, you know. And whenever you go to see him, he gets excited and faints. So I don't know whether we'll be able to do it or not. We ought to go try it anyway. Anyhow, what kind of brass band was that? Did it have a name or anything?
Joe Gabriel's Brass Band. See?
And he just used his own name for it. Do you know how big it was? Do you remember it at all?
Yeah. His band carried about seven pieces. The brass band? No, the brass band carried ten pieces. Ten pieces. That's right.
What sort of a line-up would it have? What kind of instruments would it have?

What kind of instruments would it have? Oh, trombone, val trombone, clarinet, saxophone, bass drum, alto horn, and Joe Gabriel would play the bass drum because he was a violin player in his orchestra.
So it had sort of the same line-up they're using today?
Yeah, simul, that's the only thing they used the vowel trombone, one of the trombone players.
And they had saxophones when you were a little boy?
Oh, yeah, the Deuce, you know him, the bass player? James?
Lewis James?
Yeah, he used to play the tenor saxophone.
What year would that be? How old were you?
I was about twelve years old.
Twelve years old, you were born in 1905.
So by 1917 he was playing saxophone, octet. That's right.
Saxophone and clarinet.
I heard him play a little clarinet, he sounded like he could still be good clarinet player.
Yeah, and his brother played saxophone and clarinet, Willie James. He's in California now, you never heard of him?
Not much about him, I guess.
He was younger than he was.
Did he play here in the city, Willie James?
Oh yeah, he played here. He lived there. Who did he play with? Well he played with George William, the drummer, played with his band. And he played with Louis the Man, Willie and the Deuce James.

I have to ask the one that's here about it more, Louis, I call him, huh? That's right, yeah, Louis James, yeah. The Deuce is his nickname, huh? I've never heard that before. Yeah. Oh, back to your father. What kind of a drum set did he have? I don't understand that trap foot pedal that you told about before.
It was an overhead foot pedal at that time. That's the only kind they had. And they was called overhead. And he made himself a foot pedal out of wood.
How did that work? Anything like yours today?
The foot pedal?
Uh huh.
Similar to that, but it wasn't as fast.
Well the two pieces, did it have two pieces of wood like that?
It was set up similar like a box. You see, and the wood would go down and made like a box, unless the whole is flat, the level on the floor. He made that himself.
I see. I wondered when he started playing two drums together, how? When you were very young, did he play two drums together or just one?
Two drums. That's how he'd come ahead. Yeah. What they call a trap drum. Yeah. That was when you was playing two drums. And the only sound he played one drum when he played a parade.
I know years ago they said they just played one drum at a time. They had two men.
Two men, well that was before my time. You don't remember that at all? No.
Did you ever hear the Henry Allen Brass Band years ago?
Henry Allen, Old Man Allen? Yes, I heard him.
Did any of your uncles ever play in that?
Yeah, Clay Giles. He played with me.
I saw a picture of them. And it's supposed to be him in the picture. Have you ever seen that picture? It's in the book Jazz Man?
Uh, Clay Giles? Uh huh. No, I never did see.
I wish you'd brought it with us. I just figured you'd seen it.
And I couldn't, no I haven't saw it. I mean I could definitely tell that it's him. Yeah. He had eyeglasses on. You don't remember.
I believe so.
Because I know he always wore his eyeglasses.
It's either he or the snare drummer has eyeglasses. But, uh, I'm pretty sure it's him because Peter Bococci told me. Yeah. And he would know.
Oh yeah, he know because they played together. Uh huh.
When did he play with Henry Allen? When you were a little boy or a grown man or was it?
Oh, I was a young man. I was a young man. He was in there steady with him, huh?
Yeah. Do you remember any of the guys in the band other than him?
In Allen's band? No, I don't. No more than Old Man Allen.
In the picture I think they have Jack Carey and George E. Simms, Papa Solistan, Joe Highwood.
Yeah, they.
Old Man Allen's brother, George, is playing snare.
Yeah. Okay.
I forget the rest of them.
The regular band he played in, the longest and played until he died, was the Excelsa Brass Band. That was one of the leading brass bands of the city.
Well, who had that band? Well, Gaspar.
I think Boccage, Contrell, he was a drummer, snare drummer. The Old Man Contrell.
The Old Man Contrell.
The Old Man Contrell, yeah. And which Gaspar is that?
Old Gaspar.
No, was it Old Gaspar? No, was it Old Gaspar? Which instrument did he play? Trombone.
That's Vic. Vic Gaspar, yeah.
Old Gaspar was the bass player, bass violin player, not a tuba player, bass violin player.
So Old Man Contrell was in there too, huh?

Oh yeah, he was a great drummer, one of your greatest drummers. But he played in orchestra with Piron. Well you see at those times that's how guys would play with two bands. Some guys didn't have a brass band but they had orchestra and they took practically to Goodman's for parades.
So your Uncle Clay now, did he play anything but street drums?
That's all he played, bass drums. He didn't even play trap drums.
No, that's all that at all.
Bass drums.
By trap drum what do you mean?
That's the two drums set up when you played both of them at the same time.
I wonder could he play snare in the street?
Well I wouldn't know because I never did even speak about playing a snare drum but he always played the bass drum.
Let's see, I know what else I wanted to ask you about. What about the Chalini brass band, Old Man Chalini?

Well that was mostly a band that he had a school and when he got occasionally, got jobs, well he used them. But practically he teaching all the fellows, you see. Because that's who I went to lesson on there, Old Man Chalini. He was a great teacher. He would have 40 men and if he wanted to make a mistake, he could tell who it was, stop the whole band and pick him up.
So he didn't have a regular real bass band?
No, I mean it's the scholars he would have and if it was a Kizian that he played, he would bring the band out, you know.
Who were some of his other scholars that you knew?
Well George Foer, who was my father in law, he was a bass player. He was, at the time he had so many different fellas, you know. A lot of fellas never did make it, you know.
I just wondered who some of the ones were that didn't make it later.
Oh, well they had a lot of guys. I mean it, let me see. Definitely not. Kid Howard, he was a fella I went a while, he made it. Alright. Rika, yep he made it.
Well what about your father in law, Joe H. Foer, did he play with many bands?
Oh yeah, he played, mostly he played with brass bands.
Miss Jones maybe could tell us more about that, huh?
About her father, no, because at the time that he went there she didn't know too much about music.
She was young, huh?
Yeah, well he was playing, but I mean by being young she didn't, you know, was not interested in.
What instrument did you say he played in the brass band? He played a sousaphone.
And string bass too? No, only sousaphone.
What brass bands did he work for? Remember?
Uh, Gagne's brass band. Oh yeah, the Jalma Gagne?
That's right. That guy? That's right.
That's right. That's right. That's right. That's right.
That's right. That's right.
That's right. That's right.
That's right.
That's right. He used to play with the band too.
Uh, let's see now, your father, again, didn't you say he played with some shells?

Yeah, he was a great actor, great buff dancer, comedian. 된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된
Do you remember the names of any of the shows that he might have been on?
Rabbitfoot Minstrel Shieldy. Oh yeah, the Rabbitfoot. He had a chance to be called with a Minstrel Shieldy called Black Patties.
Oh I've heard of her. She was very famous. Yeah. Did he play with, you say here, any orchestras here in the city?
Yeah.
Do you remember the names of the ones that he was playing?
Well he was called with the Ol' Arnwick band of New Orleans.
That's the brass band.
That's right. That's right. And the Silver Tone Brass Band.
Who had that?
I don't know, some was way above my time.
Seems to me they had a Silver Leaf Orchestra. They did.
This is a Silver Tone. Yeah. That was an orchestra that.
But did he play any dance jobs, I mean, other than the brass band?
Only with Joe Gabriel band, but he didn't play with bands in the Orleans, with parades.
Do you remember any drummers, early drummers way back when you were a kid, you know, that would be out in the street that impressed you? That's being good?

Yeah. Yeah. They had a fellow, Rennell Jackson. Rennell Jackson? Yeah, he's from Thibodeau. Well he was one of the young drummers. And that time, and I mean I noticed so much, you know, but he died very young. What did he play?
Snare or bass?
He played snare drum, bass drum, the ministry. He played an orchestra. He played with Joe Banks' band in Thibodeau. He played with Joe Gabriel after my daddy died.
Who were some of the other drummers you listened to when you were young?

Well Chaney Bebe, he was really a great drummer. You heard of him? Sure. He played with Celestan band. And I thought of Grady Yellow Contrell too. He was a flashy drummer but Chaney was more of a peppy drummer, I mean a younger man. They both was real great drummers.
What about your uncles now? How many of them were outstanding?

Well Oscar Giles, he was a drummer. He only played bass drum too. And Oliver Giles, he was snare drummers. He only played snare drummers. He didn't play trap drummers. And Major Giles, he was a drummer when he played trap drummers.
Who did Major play with?
Well he played with Joe Banks' band in Thibodeau.
Who was in that band? There must have been quite a few people.

Well that was the smaller band, Joe Gabriel had the biggest band. They had like five, six pieces you see. You heard talk of Adam Lombard? He was from Thibodeau, he was a great guitar player, like in Johnny Sincere class. Adam Lombard, who did he play with?
Which one?
Well he played with Joe Banks' band in Thibodeau. He still lives out there, that's his home.
Adam Lombard, huh? Yeah. Maybe we could go out and get Joe Gabriel, if we can't get him we can get Lombard.
Maybe, so I'm sure you can. Yeah we could take Punch, Russ. You'd like to do that, you know.
Yeah, that'll be a great idea. Well Punch needs to get out of him. Yeah, that'll be very good for him. Uh, so his된 major played there in Tip
Oh no, he's dead.
All your uncles?
All of them dead.
They shouldn't be too old, did they?
What the?
Your uncles, you're not, you're in your 50s, they could some of them be in their 60s. Was your father the youngest or the oldest or do you know?
My father was the youngest. Oh yeah, well they were all older than him. Yeah, that's right.
So they would be considerably older than you then. That's right.
Oh yeah.
Which one was the oldest?
You remember? Clay Giles was the oldest.
Was he much older than your father?
Oh yeah, because my father was the youngest and they had about three of them, older than my daddy and he was the oldest. That's right.
Who did Oliver Jones or Olivier, I want to know about that?

Who did he play with? Well he played with different bands in the city, he played here in the Orleans. A fellow they called Bush, Kid Bush, I don't know if you ever heard of him. You see a long time ago that's the way they used to call bands.
Yeah.
Kid Horry, Kid Rene, Kid Punch you know?
What did Bush play? He played trumpet.
Yeah.
Lawrence told me he worked with a guy called Bush Hall. That's the same one.
Lawrence Morero. That's right. That's right. That's been a pretty good band. Oh yeah. Crackley at that time, most of the bands were good.

Let's see, who else? We've got Oscar, you told me what bands he played with. Oscar, yeah. And Olivier Major played and your father Albert Hall Sr. Yeah, yeah. Okay so let's see. You mentioned on the tape before about a guy named Lawrence Randall.
Yeah, well that's who I started out playing with, the first fella there I started out with, Lawrence Randall. What instrument did he play?
He played trumpet. And who was in his band and what did they play?
Oh, Gilbert, you know what his name? Gilbert. Oh, my God. I can't call him that. That's your cousin.
What instrument did he play? He played clarinet. He still play clarinet? No, he quit playing.
And also Lawrence Randall, he quit playing. So you had a clarinet, you have a trombone or saxophone?
Uh, Joe Jones was a trombone player.
What instrument does he play? He played clarinet.
He still play clarinet? No, he quit playing. And also Lawrence
Randall, he quit playing. So you had a clarinet, you have a trombone

or saxophone? Joe Jones was a trombone player. And they got rid of him and got John Anker. You heard of him? Yeah, John Anker. And Bush Hall was the banjo player. And they got rid of him and they got Joe Jones, Joseph Jones, he played violin and banjo. But all those guys, frankly, they were playing. But now, John Anker, I don't know if he quit playing, he's around. But all those
guys I call, they all quit. And Bush Hall played banjo and trumpet

too? You say Bush Hall played in that band? Played banjo and trumpet? No. Bush, you're speaking about with Lawrence. No, Bush Hall was only a banjo player. No, he wasn't no trumpet player, that's different. That's altogether different. But Bush the trumpet player when I was speaking with you, you say Lawrence, that's altogether different. There wasn't even no relation
or nothing. And that's a bass player? You have any bass player? No, we didn't have any bass player.

No bass, piano? No piano player. I see. Well that's the first band I started playing with. After my uncle took me to Old Man's Shalow there. That was the first band. And on the way from that house I met Chris Kelly, he was playing Lawn Party and Faye Soda drummer, that was a guy I admired too, was a great drummer. And he asked me to help him carry his drum while he was playing. And so I was telling him, I was going to less and taking up drums. I'll let you work out tonight. So I got on the drum and started playing. So Chris Kelly asked me who I was playing with. I told him I wasn't playing with nobody. He started out. He let me see him. He said, Cus, do you think you can play with me tomorrow night? I said yeah. So I went on and played with him. Played on Ivorville and Murray. Homes that are big rumming place. There's a lot of Jew makers in town. He started playing over there. And these guys didn't have no passport when they came over in America. And the immigration officer was rounding them up. He broke in and stopped the band. He said, what's your name? He said, tell his name, tell you stand on the side. He thought I looked so much like a Jew maker, asked me with my name. And when I told him he said it was all right. Because he could tell by the accent that I wasn't a Jew maker. And that's when they made up that song, Going Back Home to Jamaica. When they were singing all the Jamaicans back. They didn't have their passports. They were hired away over in this country. So after that, this lady, many times Chris Kelly would blow up. So she asked me, did I think I could get a band to play for? So I got Lawrence Toker, trumpet player. And we made up a band. A fellow they called Melvin Frank. He's a clarinet player. He did. And Bill Hamilton. He's living. He don't play anymore. He's a bass player and a banjo player. But we four took over the job. And from then on, we were playing the job for these Jew makers. It wasn't, it was a house party. You would say it wasn't a dance hall. Practically they'd come in on the ship and it was mostly Jew makers would be at the dance.
I thought maybe that song had something to do with Marcus Garvey, you know. No. Because he was a Jew maker too, you know.

Yeah he was. Well, that's a lot of different in that, that I think I can kind of understand what you mean. That he was going to build ships and take the people back. But no, that was different. When this came up about those Jew makers didn't have any passports, this was at the time before that, Martha Garvey had what they call a store line club. Well that was altogether different.
So what year would that have been? That must have been pretty early. You were quite young.
Oh, let me see. What year we were married?
That would be about, we were married in 1927. That ought to have been in 1923.
uh 24. So it was after World War I anyway. Oh yeah. You were about 19 or 20 or maybe 18. Um 17. About 17. So let's see. Did you ever work with a

kid Rene? Did you ever know him? Oh yeah. I worked often and on when Joe was sick or he had two jobs. I worked with Rene, Kid Rene. They have a pretty good band? Yeah, yeah. Great band. And they had one of the top bands. Who was in it? Well Eddie, trombone player, Peter Pappy, playing clarinet. Peter Pappy playing banjo, Zeb. Johnny Prydoch playing bass at the time when I played with him. That'd be a band. Unless they had saxophone. He did. Manny Gabriel, he was playing saxophone. Violin? Have any violins? No, he can have no violins. The only violin was a big violin. This Eddie that played trombone with him, where

did he live? Oh Eddie Marsh. Eddie Marsh, he's still alive. Yeah. I think Eddie lives, I don't know, somewhere about. Oh yeah, St. Phillip. Yeah, up there. I just wondered if it was the same guy. Yeah, that's him. That looks like about the end of this reel. This is real. See, this is real too, Albert Giles. February the 24th, 1961. What kind of

jobs would a band like Rene play? Well he played advertisements, Sunday dances for clubs at home, and then he played clubs. Halls like the Corporators, Economy Hall, the Poitier Hall, the Jean-Amé Hall, the Fethian Tempher, all those old dance halls at that time. They had clubs mostly give dances, and you found men sponsored dances of their own and they charge admission. But they all had advertisements. The dances mostly was on Sunday night and Monday nights for colored people. And they would advertise and you would catch five and six bands on Sunday on trucks, what they called tailgate music. And they would meet at various corners and what we call jam and nah, they would call it bucking. And they would back the tailgates together, that's where they'd get the tailgate music from and they would buck. One would play a number and then the other one would play another number back and the people would clap to find out what band was the best. A band like Rene, and Buddy Pity, some other parts of the city, it might be Kitori and maybe Louis the Main band and was different ones, Chris Kelly and maybe Sam Morgan band. On Sundays that, because they all would advertise, it would advertise where the dance would be so that night you would know and what band you'd pick out that play the music that suits you, that you would go to the dance. But Chris Kelly and Buddy Pity was two of the greatest trumpet players on the greatest. And Chris was the greatest. He still, I've heard nobody yet play the blues like Chris Kelly, blues like Kelly's Love. If you've seen Corrine, please tell her to come home. And a lot of old blues that he played. He could get something out of the way nobody else could. He was really great. And I don't think anybody have a record that Chris Kelly made. And he was the greatest blues player I ever heard. And I've played with many trumpet players who could play the blues, but he was one of the best. To my idea. He was really great.
He was really great blues man. Who did Chris have in his band, if you'd say so?

Oh, I had George Lewis. At various times they would play together a while and Georgey Boy, certainly I, Neely Bones, at certain times they would have two jobs and split up. I saw him have jobs in using two clarinet players in the band. Do you remember who the two were? Yeah. We had Zeb, Neely, times like that, you know. Georgey Boy and George Lewis. Mostly it would be Tyne, like maybe perhaps he was short of a man, a trombone player, or either a bass player. It must have sounded good. It must have sounded good. It was good. It was, it was. They really played clarinet. All those guys, great clarinet. They really could get something out of them. Such nice tones, not like they did the tones that the new clarinet players, the young ones. And all of those guys played.
Albert's system, Albert's system, Albert's system, no Barum system.
Nowadays you can't catch a youngster. You'd have to count the one that you can find, can play an Albert's system, but they all played a Barum system.
What about those blues? Did the clarinet players specialize in blues much?

Oh yeah. That's what made it so great. The clarinet and trombone players, the way they would harmonize and make high notes and come down and low register and play. And finally the trumpet player you would take a solo and they would make stop time, what we would call after beats. And he would put mutes, his doily on his trumpet. And he would get a lot out of it without using the vowels on the trumpet. Real great. You couldn't imagine, I mean the difference, and today and at that time. Without using the vowels you said? Various notes could be made. Without using the vowels without you. You use it at your feelings. And something like Lewis. You ever see Lewis when he plays, he uses a towel over his horn all the time? He can make so many things with his lip that a fellow would think he's making some of that with his vowel. But you have to be good to do that. Some guy can't make it with the vowel, they're not making this with their lips. And that's a long time ago. The older musicians would always hide different things from another trumpet player. He didn't want them to catch on to his style. And that's why they would put their pocket handshake over their hand and like their finger, you couldn't see what he was fingering.
Who did Chris usually have on the trombone?

Well Chris used, Ambrose was one of the trombone players. That's sweet now. Harrison Bradley, he was another trombone player. Where did Harrison live? Which one is that? Harrison Bradley used to play down at Lutcher with Diddy and Billy. Oh yeah I know him. When he died. And he played with Chris, yeah. Oh yeah. They would play at certain times, you know, like they'd quit this one and go play with that one, you know. Who was the best blues trombone player? Well Jim Crow was my ideal. I loved to hear Jim play blues, take soul, Dixieland style. He filled in without playing the lead like the young trombone players would play trombone like you're playing a trumpet. But they made real cellar parts and ideas of his own to fill in and make it sound good. Instead he's going to play the lead like a trumpet. Well you wouldn't need a trumpet in the band there for trombone to play all the lead and higher notes. You want a trombone to sound like a trombone that'd make it Dixieland.
Well who would be your favorite trombone just all around?
Well I thought him and Harrison Bond was great.
Was Harrison a good man for playing by ear? Harrison Bond?

Well he played by certain numbers in Dixieland. Mostly at that time that was your best actor. They didn't have numbers come out often. You could line a number and play it so long as you played it by music. You'd line it. The guys who know how to read music, why, they would line a number and they'd get it by heart in a little while. Because at that time any man learning a number mostly be the trumpet player and he'd learn it to the rest of the men. And they got their own idea. And I think it sounds better in the music that they've written for a clarinet player or trombone or a saxophone. With their feelings and their ideas it was very great.
Who would be a great blues clarinet player at that time?
On the lead trumpet or?
No, the clarinet player. Playing blues. Not solo but all around throughout the beach.
Dixieland. Here. Georgie Boyle. He was great, huh? Yeah, he was one of the greatest.
What made him good on blues?
Well, he would get the high notes, low register and go back. He would run over it like it was nothing. It was so plain and such a good tone. Made it good.
Did he, would you call his tone right here?
Well.
Would it be like the younger clarinet player?

No, it wasn't. Smooth or rough? No, it was rough. Oh, good Dixieland is rough. Right. Dixieland is not smooth. That's what plenty of people don't understand. Dixieland is rough. It's not. That's where Piro and bands like Sam Morgan, had what we call soft pedal bands. They would play such smooth and nice. Well that wasn't considered as Dixieland. They were stock bands. They played stock music. But Dixieland was played from the heart, soul and mind. That's what made it so good. But it was rough.
Sam wasn't rough then. His band was smooth. Real smooth. When was that? That was the old Sam Morgan band before?

Izel. Oh, Izel took it there. Before Izel took it. Oh, you see Izel was playing second trumpet, what they called second trumpet, but in their band Sam and Izel made the same thing. It was great. Two great men to make the same thing at the same time. I never could understand. It was great. It wasn't a very seldom any second was made. Mike, they would make the same thing at the same time. It sounded good, huh? I mean, it sounded like one, but so heavy, you know.
So which band was seventh
The Young Morgan with Sam added on or was it the old original Morgan band?
The Young Morgan band was the roughest after Sam got out of the picture, he got sick and when Isaiah took it over and then they began to get rough.
Well who was in that original band?

Well he had a pretty good brass band.
Were they readers or with Long By Head or what?
Yeah. Practically they had men in their reds. Men like Manuel Perez played with Rene band. He was a wonderful reader. Old Man Pico played with Rene's funeral. Old Man Alfred. Which Old Man Alfred?
Is that Jim or Willie?
The Old Man. The Grandfather of Percy and Willie and Earl.
Their Father.
Their Father.
Yeah. Well you know, I didn't think Rene was a good reader or anything. Could he read those funeral marches?

Yeah. He could read pretty good. Yeah. He could read pretty good. And in times I mean it wasn't complicated. Well they played the same funeral march for ten, fifteen years, the same number. I mean if a fellow couldn't learn that he would be a real poor reader, you know. He'd take it from your home, my God, to thee. Now that's a number like home sweet home. It never dies out. Why, you play that, close to walk with thee, what a friend we have in Jesus. Now those numbers you could keep it for twenty years. When you're going with the body you play those numbers. That's not very long. Then after the funeral, I didn't even ramble and when the saints go marching in and on jazz and numbers. So that's easy to get over. If you had four funeral marches, why you had it made.
And they wouldn't play the real hard ones and they'd play some of them like that. That's pretty easy.
That's true. That's what I'm speaking about.
Now some of those Eureka things sound pretty complicated.
Oh yeah they does because they got a standard band, but another band could make out, you understand. Yeah they have some nice funeral marches because they're standard.
Tuxedo has some hard ones.

Yeah they does too. Well they're both the two standard bands you had, brass bands. So it's practically that they could rehearsal a number with the other old ones, they got back and say in three months they could play a new one. It wouldn't be hard to get that now, in fact they could wake on another one.
Who else would Rene have in his funeral band, his brass band?
Like what?
You had mentioned Manuel on trumpet. Yeah.

Any of those? He used to use Poiseum Elford, Lee Collins, yeah he at various certain times, just like I say you know, that play. He used Harrison Bones on trombone, Jim Crow and other trombone players. Morris French, and Sean Warren, Ambrose at certain times.
Who would Chris use? Would he have pretty steady men or not?

No, Chris he, it's like I told you, he didn't have steady men either. Chris would play with you tonight and have a funeral tomorrow and be using somebody else. Because he wasn't a standard, I mean a band that looked forward to a band.
all he wanted a job and his name was good and if he felt like he wanted to use somebody else he'd go and use him. That you wasn't regular but he appreciated when he would use you, it was all right.
So they had brass bands like that that were playing funerals that weren't standard, they had quite a few little jump up bands.

That's right. Yeah, they would have, sometimes they would have five funerals in one day. And long years back practically more people had bands because they had societies that furnished and paid for the band and three or four members died and some of them would be belongs to three societies that give the band. Some of them would want two bands and some would give the money to the winner, what they would get the third band with and some would take the money for two of the bands and let one band play. Because all of those organizations used to have bands.
What was the biggest one you ever saw for a funeral?
Well the biggest one I saw was Silly Stan. They tell me that Piku's was the biggest but I didn't see Piku.
Did you see Chris Gellis funeral?

Yeah. It was a big funeral like Silly Stan. Now it seems that they make more of the older Dixieland men than they did at that time. They didn't make as much of them as they're doing today. They're more understanding and realize what they're losing now. At that time they didn't practically know. Now they're all dying out and they can feel it that there's nobody to take their place.
Well they understand it after you're dead. They don't understand it before you die most of the time.
That's right too.
Many of them pass on and they never.
Give it a thought. Until it happens.
Until he died.
And some people had forgotten about Piku until he died. And when he died then they realized that what a great man he has been.
Well they never said nobody hardly cared when Harrison Bradley died. And they didn't make anything and he was with a lot of those famous bands too.

Well that's what I'm saying. That the people of the day they are, it's a lot different from years ago. That's why they make so much over a guy now because they just realize at that time after you died they didn't make over you. Well now they are making over you after you die.

I was just wondering on that, you know, when you were talking about the societies and all that and I know most of the time when musicians die today they aren't members of societies and the union furnishes the band. Did more musicians used to belong to societies in the old days?

Well at that time the union wasn't in demand and every musician didn't belong to the union and it wasn't as particular. You could play with a band, a man wasn't in the union and nobody got farm or nothing. They hadn't gotten to that stage. I understand now the bands that you see, that gets by me if the union are paying for those bands because I don't think they did. The union gives $1,000 to the widow and she have to pay for that out of that. Those bands, you see, I wouldn't know, I wouldn't want to say it, I don't know, but I think somebody had to pay for Piku bands. The union don't give the band, but in the time of speaking about the organizations that's what made them have so many bands because that money was set aside for the members or tax, when a member died that was put for the band. But now all those societies have broken up and if a musician had died, after a long time ago, any time a musician had died that the rest of the musicians would volunteer and play for nothing. They wouldn't wait. You would have so many musicians be walking over one another. They'd play for nothing. That was an honor to play. But now as soon as somebody died, a union musician couldn't go play for nothing. The union wouldn't allow that. They'd make a rammer with the wither and tell her that you want to get a band, or you get the tuxedo band, or the Eureka band, it costs you so much and so much, and they'd reduct that out of that thousand dollars.
I also was wondering, you were talking about pickup bands, what did they used to wear to play funeral?

Well practically a guy who played in a funeral, if it was a funeral, any band, or pickup, put a white shirt on and a musician cap and blue pants. And his uniform didn't have no name on it, you understand? If you had a name, it didn't make any difference. Because drummers carry on a drum the name of the band that they played with one time, worth standing, and they never took the name off and they'd be playing with another band with that same name on the band. You know that's logic. I didn't like the stem on that. You know they pick up, consider that, see Dick you play? So I got a little jump up job, a little funeral. Albert you play? No. I said, well that's what makes it, see, be a pickup band, you know, get different fellas and they make up a band. That was it at that time. Every time they have a funeral, now that's why they get the Eureka or the tuxedo band, because they stand at the union call for them, because that's up to them. But they wouldn't want us to go out and make a pickup band, because they got a stand at band, they hire them.
I'm afraid that's it. That's it? Just about, we're out of tape just about, so we better call it short. Okay. Tip stuff

segments.title: Opening of reel one and introductions
segments.summary: Dick Allen gives the date and place, and Jiles and the others in the room give their names.

segments.title: Grandfather Frank Giles and father in New Orleans bands
segments.summary: Jiles's grandfather played drums in the Civil War; his father lived in Thibodeaux but was hired for Carnival and parades.

segments.title: Joe Gabriel's orchestra and brass band
segments.summary: Gabriel led an orchestra and a ten-piece brass band, and Jiles describes the instrumentation.

segments.title: Lewis James, Willie James and saxophone in the 1910s
segments.summary: Lewis James played tenor sax and clarinet by about 1917; his brother Willie James played with other bands.

segments.title: Father's homemade foot pedal and two-drum trap set
segments.summary: Father built a wooden foot pedal and played two drums together, but one drum in parades.

segments.title: Uncle Clay Giles in Henry Allen's brass band
segments.summary: Clay Giles played in Old Man Allen's band, and they discuss a picture of its members.

segments.title: Excelsior Brass Band, Contrell, and Clay's bass drum
segments.summary: Clay played bass drum in the Excelsior band; Old Man Contrell and Gaspar are discussed, and the meaning of trap drums.

segments.title: Lessons and the school band of Old Man Chaligny
segments.summary: Chaligny ran a school band and taught many students, including Jiles, Kid Howard and his future father-in-law.

segments.title: Father-in-law, the sousaphone player, and his brass bands
segments.summary: His father-in-law played sousaphone in brass bands such as Gagne's.

segments.title: Father as a comedian and the bands he played with
segments.summary: His father was an actor and dancer who worked minstrel shows and brass bands including Silver Tone and Joe Gabriel's.

segments.title: Early drummers Jiles admired as a boy
segments.summary: Rennell Jackson, Chaney and Grady Contrell are named as drummers who impressed him.

segments.title: Uncles Oscar, Oliver and Major Giles, and Thibodeaux bands
segments.summary: His uncles were drummers; Major played with Joe Banks's band, and they mention guitarist Adam Lombard and the family order.

segments.title: Oliver Giles and Kid Bush's band
segments.summary: Oliver played in different city bands, with Kid Bush among those named.

segments.title: Lawrence Randall, Jiles's first band
segments.summary: Jiles started with trumpeter Lawrence Randall's band, and they sort out its clarinet, trombone and banjo players.

segments.title: Meeting Chris Kelly and playing for the Jamaicans' house parties
segments.summary: Jiles filled in for Chris Kelly's drummer, then formed a band with Lawrence Toker, Melvin Frank and Bill Hamilton to play for Jamaican sailors.

segments.title: Marcus Garvey question and dating the early work
segments.summary: Allen asks whether the song relates to Garvey; Jiles says no, and they work out the date as about 1923.

segments.title: Working with Kid Rene's band
segments.summary: Jiles subbed for Kid Rene's drummer; the band's personnel are named and the reel ends.

segments.title: Dance halls, advertising trucks, tailgate bucking, and Chris Kelly's blues
segments.summary: Jobs for bands like Rene's, Sunday tailgate competitions between bands, and why Chris Kelly was the greatest blues trumpeter.

segments.title: Chris Kelly's clarinetists and how blues were played
segments.summary: Clarinetists in Kelly's band, their tone, and how clarinet, trombone and muted trumpet handled the blues.

segments.title: Trombonists with Chris Kelly and Jim Crow's style
segments.summary: Ambrose, Harrison Bradley and Jim Crow are discussed, and how a trombone should fill in Dixieland.

segments.title: Georgie Boyle on blues clarinet and why Dixieland is rough
segments.summary: Georgie Boyle is called a great blues clarinetist; Jiles argues real Dixieland is rough while Piron and Sam Morgan played smooth stock music.

segments.title: The Sam Morgan band and its later roughness
segments.summary: Sam and Isaiah Morgan's trumpets, the original personnel, and how the band got rougher when Isaiah took over.

segments.title: Piano and drum house parties and Frazier pianists
segments.summary: Piano and drum jobs at lawn parties were plentiful; Jiles worked with Mitchell and Simon Frazier and a pianist called Herman.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's shifting band and its drummers
segments.summary: Petit used changing sidemen; Jiles names clarinetists, trombonists, drummers, bassists and sax, and prefers clarinet to sax.

segments.title: Papa Celestin's 1941 band and its members
segments.summary: Jiles played with Celestin for a few months in 1941 until Celestin was hurt, and names the sidemen.

segments.title: Playing with Albert Burbank, then leading his own band
segments.summary: Jiles was with Burbank when Bill Russell recorded him, then led a small band with Joe Snider, Earl Bourne and Lester Lewis.

segments.title: Club Sands and the small band with Joe Snider
segments.summary: Jiles played a three-piece job at Club Sands with Snider, and they recall the others in the band.

segments.title: Playing with Burbank and Moran uptown and at the Dandy Inn
segments.summary: Jiles recalls the Burbank band with Moran, Talbidge and Lester Lewis, the nights at Messmer's near the Dandy Inn, and an uptown spot they cannot name.

segments.title: Order of Jiles's bands: Randall, Kelly, Toker, Rene Parker
segments.summary: They sort out when he played with Lawrence Toker and Rene Parker; the Toker band held together about 1925 and again after the war.

segments.title: Who he played with around World War II
segments.summary: Jiles gives the order: Rene Parker, then Toker, then Albert Burbank around the war years.

segments.title: Rene Parker's band and the trombonist-bassist nicknamed Fire
segments.summary: Rene Parker's band had John Anker, Solomon Smith on banjo, Clemens on bass or trombone, and a sax player but no piano.

segments.title: Where Allen met him: Burbank, Lionel and the Happy Landing
segments.summary: Jiles traces his bands after the Russell recordings, including the Happy Landing job with Lionel.

segments.title: Leading the Happy Landing band and its changing members
segments.summary: After a dispute Jiles took over Israel's band at the Happy Landing and hired Andrew Morgan; he explains how sidemen swapped between bands.

segments.title: Lester Lewis and playing with Billy and De De
segments.summary: Lester Lewis is still alive; Jiles played a year or two with Billy and De De at the Silver Star and Lutcher.

segments.title: English revival bands and King Colyer
segments.summary: Jiles thinks Ken Colyer played closest to old Dixieland and that Chris Barber's band skipped around when playing a rag.

segments.title: Dixieland versus jazz versus ragtime
segments.summary: Jiles explains how Dixieland, jazz and ragtime differ and why ragtime has to be played from written music.

segments.title: Funerals he played and with which bands
segments.summary: Jiles played funerals with Kid Rene, Chris Kelly, Tuxedo and pickup bands, but never Eureka.

segments.title: Kid Rene's funeral brass band and the funeral marches
segments.summary: Rene's brass band used good readers; Jiles describes the few funeral marches and the men Rene used.

segments.title: Chris Kelly's pickup funeral bands and burial societies
segments.summary: Kelly had no steady men, and societies once paid for several bands at one funeral.

segments.title: The biggest funerals and honoring musicians late
segments.summary: Celestin's was the biggest he saw; he says people only appreciate old Dixieland men once they have died.

segments.title: Societies, the union and funeral bands
segments.summary: Jiles explains how societies paid for bands, musicians once played for free, and how the union now handles funeral bands.

segments.title: Pickup funeral bands and uniforms
segments.summary: Pickup funeral players wore white shirts, caps and blue pants with no band name.

segments.title: End of tape
segments.summary: Allen says the tape is nearly out and ends the session.
